judgments.title: KAVITAH A/P SUBRAMANIAM v Jhayanthira A/l Palanivelu
judgments.catchwords: Matrimonial law — Nullity of marriage — Voidable marriage — Non-consummation owing to wilful refusal of respondent — Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976, s 70(b) Matrimonial law — Jurisdiction — Marriage registered under the Act — Both parties residing in Malaysia when proceedings commenced — Requirements of s 67 satisfied Matrimonial law — Undefended nullity petition — Respondent served but entering no appearance — Decree affecting personal status not granted by default, consent or sympathy — Court required independently to scrutinise evidence and establish statutory ground Matrimonial law — Pleading — Petition referring generally to s 70 without specifying applicable limb — Facts pleaded disclosing only non-consummation attributable to respondent — Defect one of label rather than substance — Petition treated as proceeding under s 70(b) Matrimonial law — Non-consummation — Two statutory elements — Proof of absence of consummation and proof of prescribed cause — Words “owing to” imposing requirement of causation — Non-consummation alone insufficient Matrimonial law — Wilful refusal — Settled and definite decision made without just excuse — Refusal may be inferred from proven conduct — Respondent’s silence, consent or non-objection not by itself proof of refusal — Detailed factual matrix required Matrimonial law — Customary and religious solemnisation — Parties agreeing before civil registration that conjugal life would commence only after Hindu customary ceremony — Refusal to undertake agreed indispensable step capable of constituting wilful refusal to consummate — Refusal of indispensable means amounting to refusal of the end Matrimonial law — Antecedent agreement concerning solemnisation — Agreement postponing cohabitation and consummation until customary or religious ceremony neither illegal, immoral nor contrary to public policy — No distinction in principle between belief founded on custom and belief founded on religion Matrimonial law — Wilful refusal to proceed with antecedent ceremony — Conditions — Genuinely shared pre-marital understanding proved by evidence — Settled and definite refusal without just excuse — Petitioner remaining ready and willing — Refusal being operative cause of non-consummation — Mutual abandonment insufficient Matrimonial law — Express demand and refusal — Whether indispensable — No legal requirement for specific demand for ceremony or intercourse followed by express rebuff — Refusal capable of proof entirely through conduct — Formal demand unnecessary where futile or exposing petitioner to risk of further violence Evidence — Inference from cumulative conduct — Prolonged failure to prepare for customary ceremony — Self-induced loss of employment and continuing unemployment — Repeated physical violence — Solicitation of commercial sexual services — Conduct compelling inference of settled decision not to proceed with ceremony or consummate marriage Matrimonial law — Just excuse — Self-induced impecuniosity arising from absenteeism and drunkenness not excusing failure to proceed — No illness, incapacity or other supervening circumstance established Matrimonial law — Causation — Customary ceremony being agreed gateway to conjugal life — Ceremony not occurring because of respondent’s refusal — Petitioner remaining ready and willing — Non-consummation caused by respondent’s wilful refusal Matrimonial law — Supervening reluctance of petitioner — Fear for health and safety arising from respondent’s misconduct — Reluctance neither converting matter into mutual refusal nor breaking chain of causation — Reluctance founded upon just excuse Matrimonial law — Nullity and divorce — Distinct statutory remedies — Nullity not available judgments.title: EXTRA EXCEL (MALAYSIA) SDN BHD v QUEK PECK KEOW
judgments.catchwords: Section 10(1) of the Arbitration Act 2005 - whether section 10(1) of the AA 2005 required the courts below to determine for themselves the existence and operability of the arbitration agreement, or whether that question ought to have been left to the arbitral tribunal under section 18 and the doctrine of kompetenz-kompetenz - whether the 2nd Stay Application and OS 2 are barred by res judicata or issue estoppel arising from the April 2022 Decision - the proper construction of Clause 1.3 in its November 2019 form, and in particular whether it ever entitled the Appellant to commence arbitration against its own distributor - whether the June 2021 amendment to Clause 1.3 could, consistently with ordinary contractual principles, be applied retrospectively to a dispute that had already crystallised and was already the subject of litigation - whether the Appellant had, in any event, taken a step in the proceedings within the meaning of section 10(1), disentitling it to a stay - whether Clause 1.3 is void, in whole or in part, under sections 24 and 29 of the Contracts Act 1950, because it caps the Respondent’s recoverable damages - whether the Appellant’s unilateral right to appoint the sole arbitrator renders the arbitration agreement void, or offends natural justice - whether the finding that the Appellant acted in bad faith was properly made without a trial.

judgments.title: Pendakwa Raya & ors v Julasiri Bin Akilmara
judgments.catchwords: Offence under section 39B(1)(a) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 read together with section 34 of the Penal Code - Whether the trial judge should have informed at the close of the prosecution's case, that the defence was being called upon to answer a case of actual trafficking or presumed trafficking? - Overwhelming evidence proved the elements of custody, control, and knowledge - Actual possession of the impugned drugs was established - Section 180 (1) and (4) of the Criminal Procedure Code - Procedure after conclusion of case for prosecution - No statutory or legal requirement to state the presumption when calling for the defence - Formal verbal label for an evidentiary rule at the close of the prosecution's case is unnecessary - Statutory presumption of trafficking under section 37(da)(xvi) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952 - Section 422 of the Criminal Procedure Code - Not vitiate the conviction - No miscarriage of justice - Failure either to make or to record such a finding does not ipso facto - The law does not require a mini-judgment or detailed legal reasons at the close of the prosecution’s case

parties.label: DEFENDAN
names: EE KEE NOODLE MANUFACTURER SDN BHD

judgments.catchwords: Civil Procedure – Pleadings – clerical error in date of incident; binding effect of pleadings; amendment of pleadings; prejudice to defendant. Evidence – Burden of Proof – obligation on plaintiff to prove causation; insufficiency of inference; speculation vs inference. Evidence – Hearsay – inadmissibility of hearsay testimony; reliance on unverified translation; probative value of fire report. Expert Evidence – qualifications of fire investigator; compliance with Order 40A ROC 2012; deficiencies in methodology; adverse inference under s.114(g) Evidence Act. Negligence – Duty of Care – neighbouring occupiers; breach and causation; machine not operational at material time. Res Ipsa Loquitur – applicability of maxim; rebuttal of presumption by defendant’s evidence. Rylands v Fletcher – non-natural use of land; fire as a “thing” escaping; applicability in industrial context. Fire – Cause and Origin – reliability of official fire report; technical evidence on oil and machine specifications; alternative sources of ignition. Damages – Proof of Loss – quantum of RM30,732,303.80; audited records; insurance recovery; attribution of losses. Civil Liability – Industrial Fire – liability between neighbouring factories; accident classification; failure to establish causation.

judgments.title: SUPERMIX (MALAYSIA) SDN BHD v PRESTASI MEWAH HOLDINGS SDN BHD
judgments.catchwords: An appeal has been filed by the appellant, who was the defendant in the Sessions Court, against a decision rendered by the learned Sessions Court Judge. The defendant's counterclaim for the balance of the security deposit after deducting the rental payments was also dismissed. Upon termination of the Tenancy Agreement, the defendant was required to perform repairs and restorations, which the defendant did. The plaintiff, however, claims that they weren't done satisfactorily. This allegation has no basis, as the parties agreed to deem the repair and rehabilitation works to be final, and there shall be no further claims, disputes, or causes of action against the defendant following completion. As a result, the appeal has been allowed.

judgments.catchwords: Review jurisdiction - Rule 137 of the Rules of the Federal Court 1995 -Inherent powers of Federal Court – All sentences passed to be in accordance with the law – Avoiding miscarriage of justice - Exceptional circumstances - Fresh evidence of prisoner’s death following whipping. Constitutional Law - Federal Constitution - Articles 5(1), 8(1) and 8(2) Fundamental liberties - Life and personal liberty - Human dignity - Equal protection of the law - Whether it is in violation of medical ethics for medical officer to be participate in the execution of whipping. Judicial whipping - Corporal punishment - Whether judicial whipping amounts to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment (“CIDT”) - Whether punishment of whipping is inconsistent with constitutional protection of life, dignity and bodily integrity. Whether whipping is disproportionate and therefore contrary to Article 8(1) - Whether exemption of women from whipping constitutes prohibited discrimination on ground only of gender is contrary to Art 8(2) - Intelligible differentia. Whether whipping is against Art. 5 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (“UDHR”) and the ASEAN Human Rights Declaration in its prohibitions against CIDT - Whether whipping is against customary international law.

judgments.title: SUHANA BINTI MOHAMED & ors v ROSLI BIN AWANG
judgments.catchwords: DAMAGES: Fatal accident – Dependency claim – Claim brought by wife and children of deceased – Wife alleged that deceased’s salary contributed substantially towards household expenses, including maintenance and education of children – Deceased’s income – Whether deceased’s monthly income should have been assessed at RM3,000.00 instead of RM2,000.00 – Whether one-third of multiplicand ought to have been deducted for deceased’s own living expenses – Whether deduction could be made in absence of proof or admission of deceased’s living expenses – Whether conventional one-third deduction was applicable. ROAD TRAFFIC: Negligence – Road Accident – Ascertaining liability – Collision between motorcycle and motorcar – Vehicles travelling in the same direction – Respondent’s motorcar intended to turn left into an exit – Absence of any independent eyewitness – Damage to motorcar confined to its left side, comprising a dented left front door, shattered left window and broken left side mirror – Damage to motorcycle being comparatively minor – Absence of brake marks or tyre marks attributable to either vehicle – Res ipsa loquitur – Whether oral evidence amplified or contradicted police report – Whether alleged inconsistency between police report and pleadings was material – Whether deceased was contributorily negligent – Whether equal apportionment of liability was justified.
